items.explanation: Herblock's cartoon shows Eisenhower offering only a meek 'Have a care, sir' while McCarthy brandishes his smear tactics — criticizing the president for refusing to confront McCarthyism directly even as he found the senator's methods 'reprehensible.'
options: (A) McCarthy and Eisenhower cooperated effectively to halt the spread of Communism at home.
(B) McCarthy went too far when he accused Eisenhower himself of Communist sympathies.
(C) McCarthy wisely guarded the nation while Eisenhower blindly ignored security threats.
(D) Eisenhower's public criticisms of McCarthy's crusade were feeble and inadequate.
items.stem: [Image description: Herblock, 'Have a care, sir,' Washington Post, 1954. Senator Joseph McCarthy on the left, menacing and aggressive; President Dwight D. Eisenhower on the right, offering only a mild rebuke.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

items.explanation: McCarthy's Wheeling speech claiming a list of State Department Communists came in February 1950, months before the Korean War began that June; the war's atmosphere of crisis amplified him, and his fall came with the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings after the armistice.
options: (A) The postwar wave of labor strikes in 1945–1946.
(B) The Korean War and its atmosphere of national-security crisis.
(C) The 'massive resistance' campaign of white Southerners against desegregation.
(D) The Cuban Missile Crisis.
items.stem: McCarthy's peak power and influence coincided with which of the following?

items.explanation: The McCarthy–Eisenhower split was over methods, not ends: both opposed Communism, but disagreed on whether reckless accusations, blacklists, and loyalty investigations were acceptable — the recurring American debate over acceptable means (cf. the 1920s Red Scare, the court-packing fight, the Patriot Act).
options: (A) Continuing debates over the proper role of political parties.
(B) Continuing debates over political means and ends.
(C) Continuing debates over executive versus legislative power.
(D) Continuing debates over federal regulation of the economy.
items.stem: The ideas in the cartoon most directly reflect which continuity in twentieth-century American history?

items.explanation: Savio's December 1964 Sproul Hall sit-in address — students as 'raw material' refusing to be processed by the university 'machine' — became the defining text of the Berkeley Free Speech Movement and, by extension, the student New Left.
options: (A) The migration of Americans to the Sunbelt states in the postwar decades.
(B) The student New Left and the Free Speech Movement.
(C) The organized labor movement.
(D) The conservative New Right.
items.stem: Savio's address is a landmark text of which movement?
items.stimulus: Mario Savio told the Berkeley crowd in December 1964 that if the university was a firm run by regents and its president, students were merely its raw material — and that when a machine's operation became odious, people could no longer take part even passively and had to throw their bodies upon its gears to stop it. — paraphrased from Mario Savio's 'sit-in address,' UC Berkeley, December 1964

items.explanation: The New Left — veterans of Freedom Summer and campus activism — attacked Cold War liberalism from the left, arguing that the Warren Court and the Great Society, for all their achievements, left racial and economic structures fundamentally untransformed.
options: (A) Conservatives mobilized against juvenile delinquency and the decline of the traditional family.
(B) Artists and writers withdrew from politics into abstract expression.
(C) Activists on the left charged liberals with failing to transform the status quo.
(D) Working-class militants rebelled against complacent union leadership.
items.stem: Savio's speech best reflects which broader trend of the 1960s?

items.explanation: The Free Speech Movement drew on the baby-boom surge in college enrollment and the postwar expansion of higher education: mass universities, filled with middle-class students, became the staging ground for student activism.
options: (A) An employment boom in heavy industry.
(B) The collapse of family farming and the rise of agribusiness.
(C) The baby-boom expansion of higher education and social mobility.
(D) The growing visibility of immigrant neighborhoods in big cities.
items.stem: Which economic or demographic shift is most closely tied to the movement Savio's speech exemplified?

items.explanation: By 1967 King charged that Vietnam was devouring the Great Society, contrasting the vast sums spent per enemy killed with the pittance spent per person classified as poor — the war escalating while the fight against poverty was scaled back. His antiwar stand ruptured his alliance with LBJ.
options: (A) The federal government's refusal to desegregate the armed forces.
(B) The Great Society's failure against poverty as Vietnam consumed funds.
(C) The Republican Party's fixation on foreign policy over domestic needs.
(D) Congress's refusal to pass any meaningful civil-rights legislation.
items.stem: King's 1967 speech was most directly a response to which of the following?
items.stimulus: In a 1967 address, Martin Luther King Jr. argued that widening the Vietnam War was narrowing domestic welfare programs, making the poor bear the heaviest burdens both at the front and at home; the nation was escalating the war in Vietnam while de-escalating the fight against poverty. — paraphrased from Martin Luther King Jr., 1967 address on Vietnam

items.explanation: King's linkage of the war to poverty and racism placed him in the growing antiwar movement, which swelled as casualties mounted and television brought the war into American living rooms.
options: (A) The growth of the antiwar movement as escalation deepened U.S. involvement.
(B) A refusal by 1960s protest movements to connect foreign and domestic policy.
(C) The success of anti-Communist propaganda in silencing dissent.
(D) A shift by the civil-rights movement from nonviolence to armed resistance.
items.stem: The excerpt best reflects which of the following trends?
